paras: The lynching of old man Kelly was the reported hanging of the elder member of the Kelly family of "No Man's Land" by pursuing vigilantes in the Texas Panhandle, described in dispatches dated January 2 to 4, 1888. According to these reports, the vigilantes overtook him after a long chase, hanged him, let him down until he confessed that his family had killed and robbed nine men and two women, and hanged him again. Papers from West Virginia to Montana ran it as the end of the Kelly murder case, but the Wichita Eagle called the Kelly stories "fabrications."

The Kellys, a father, mother, son and daughter, kept a "half way house" near Oak City in No Man's Land frequented by travelers with money. The Custer Chronicle named the old man as William, aged about fifty-five. In mid-December, after a Chicago firm asked about a missing drummer, searchers reported finding his body and others in the cellar and around the barn.

The family had passed through Beaver City days earlier, saying they were bound for New Mexico. A posse of twenty citizens followed their trail along Palo Duro Creek and south toward Wheeler County, Texas.

About noon on "Thursday last" the pursuers sighted the family, who left their wagon and mounted the horses they had been leading. After a two-hour chase Mrs. Kelly's horse fell; the son and daughter were then halted and hanged from a tree, while the old man, on a better horse, rode on. After three more hours the posse sighted him, fired two shots when he refused to halt, and surrounded him.

Told he had a short time to live, Kelly asked about his wife and children, and the vigilantes' leader pointed to the limb of a tree. In the statement attributed to him, Kelly said he had come from Pennsylvania, opened a tavern near Beaver City, and left for Texas after talk of foul play, denying knowledge of any killings. The band hanged him with his hands tied and let him down, and by their account he then said the whole family was equally guilty of killing and robbing nine men and two women. He was hanged again and left hanging; a gold watch marked "I. A. T." was reported found on him, and Taylor was named as one of the missing men.
No vigilante is named, and no report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution was found.

A Wichita dispatch, in which the mother and son had already been killed, appeared in the Wheeling Register on January 4, the Daily Yellowstone Journal of Miles City on January 6, and the Hillsboro, Ohio, News-Herald on January 12 as "Old Kelly Caught and Lynched." A special to the Little Rock Gazette from Harold, Texas, with the tree limb and the watch, ran in the Emporia Weekly News on January 5 as "A Terror Hanged" and in the Western Kansas World on January 14 as "The Last of the Kellys."

A longer Fort Elliott, Texas, narrative of the whole pursuit ran in the Waterbury Evening Democrat on January 3, the Waco Daily Examiner on January 6, and the Custer Chronicle on January 14. These papers treated the hanging as deserved: the Fort Elliott dispatch said the Kellys "have quickly met the vengeance they deserved," the Waco Examiner headed its story "Hanged at Last," and the Custer Chronicle wrote that they "Receive Their Due Reward." Kelly's statement and confession reached print only as the vigilantes' account, with no named witness.

On January 7 the Wichita Eagle called the Kansas City Times' Wichita correspondent "a searcher after notoriety" paid for "fabrications." It said he had first sent Kelly to Mexico and then had him overtaken by vigilantes and "dispatched after the regulation fashion." The Harold and Fort Elliott versions ran under other datelines, though none names a participant.

Accounts of the family's end also differ: a Wichita dispatch of December 31 had the mother shot and the son dragged to death after their dugout was fired, while the Fort Elliott narrative had the son and daughter hanged. The year Kelly said he reached Kansas is printed as 1869 in the Harold version and 1879 in the Wheeling Register.

reader.title: Lynching of old man Kelly
bases: A band of vigilantes from Beaver City was reported to have run down the elder Kelly and hanged him for murders charged to his family (A1, A4, A5).

As reported, a posse of about twenty vigilantes hanged Kelly without legal process for murders charged to his family (A1, A4, A5, A9); the Wichita Eagle called the Wichita correspondent's Kelly stories fabrications (A7) and no local confirmation or participant name appears, so the killing itself is not independently established.

Wichita, Harold and Fort Elliott dispatches agree that vigilantes hanged the old man (A1, A2, A4), but the Wichita Eagle dismissed the Kansas City Times correspondent's Kelly stories as fabrications (A7).

accounts.label: Wichita dispatch
accounts.gist: After the mother and son were killed, vigilantes overtook the escaped old man after three hours, hanged and let him down until he confessed to nine men and two women killed, then hanged him again.

accounts.label: Harold, Texas special to the Gazette
accounts.gist: Vigilantes caught the only survivor of the family near Harold, heard his denial, hanged him, let him down to confess, hanged him again and found a gold watch marked 'I. A. T.'

accounts.label: Fort Elliott narrative
accounts.gist: A posse of twenty from Beaver City hanged the son and daughter, then tracked the old man three hours, fired on him, and hanged him after his statement.

accounts.label: Wichita Eagle
accounts.gist: The Kansas City Times' Wichita correspondent invented the Kelly stories, first sending the old man to Mexico and then having vigilantes dispatch him.

framing.detail: Fort Elliott dispatch: the Kellys 'have quickly met the vengeance they deserved'.
Custer Chronicle headline 'The Kelly Family, Rivals of the Benders, Receive Their Due Reward'.

Wichita and Harold dispatches reprinted under headings such as 'A Terror Hanged' and 'Old Kelly Caught and Lynched'.
Wichita Eagle mocked the Kelly stories as a correspondent's 'fabrications' in 'regular wild west style'.
